title: Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La day trip planner
meta_description: Plan the Gangtok to Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir and Nathu La day: timings, permits, vehicle costs, altitude, what to wear and how to avoid wasted money.
summary: The Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir and Nathu La trip is a full day from Gangtok, leaving at about 7 am and back by 3–4 pm. You need a protected area permit through a registered agent, and Nathu La is for Indian citizens only, Wednesday to Sunday. A car costs ₹6,500–9,000 with Nathu La, indicative 2026.

sections.heading: The day at a glance
paras: This is East Sikkim's most popular day out, and for good reason. In about 55 km the road climbs from Gangtok at 1,650 m to Nathu La at 4,310 m, through forest, alpine scrub and bare rock, past a glacial lake and an army shrine, to a pass on the India–China border. It is also a long, cold and high day, and the timings matter more than most people expect.
Here is a typical schedule. Your driver may change the order, often doing Nathu La first and the lake on the way back, because the army limits how late visitors can stay at the pass.

sections.heading: Permits and the right day
paras: You need a Protected Area Permit for Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La, and you cannot apply for it yourself. A registered Gangtok travel agent or your hotel's agent files it with one photo ID copy and two passport photos per person. Hand these over the evening before for Tsomgo, and a day ahead, often by early afternoon, for Nathu La.

Nathu La is open only to Indian citizens, and as we understand it only Wednesday to Sunday; it is closed to tourists on Monday and Tuesday. Operators usually will not take children under 5 to Nathu La. Foreign nationals can visit Tsomgo Lake on a day permit through an agent, usually in a group of at least two, but cannot go on to Nathu La. Snow, landslides or security alerts can close the pass on any day. Check current status before you travel, and see our permits guide for the full rules.

sections.heading: Vehicle and what it costs
paras: Only Gangtok-registered tourist vehicles with the right papers can run this route, so a car hired in Siliguri cannot take you. Most trips use a Bolero, Scorpio, Xylo or similar, carrying up to about five passengers. Book through your hotel or a registered agent, and confirm in writing what is included: permit, waiting time and all stops.

Our indicative 2026 ranges are below. In 2024 the Sikkim government published fixed and maximum fares for these packages by vehicle class, after complaints of overcharging; ask your agent to show you the current chart, and check current status before you travel.
list: Whole car, Tsomgo and Baba Mandir: ₹4,500–6,500 per vehicle.
Whole car, Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La: ₹6,500–9,000 per vehicle.
Shared seat on a Tsomgo tour: ₹800–1,300 per person.
Nathu La permit: around ₹200 per person, often included in the car price.
Coat and boot hire at the roadside shops: ₹100–300 per item.
Yak ride or photo at Tsomgo: ₹300–600.
Tea, Maggi noodles and momos at the lake stalls: ₹30–150 per item.

sections.heading: Altitude: how to stay well
paras: The biggest risk on this trip is not the road; it is the height. You climb more than 2,600 m in about three hours and spend time above 4,000 m with no chance to acclimatise. Most healthy adults feel only a mild headache or breathlessness, but some feel worse, and acute mountain sickness can begin above 3,000 m.

Do not do this trip on your first day in Sikkim. Spend at least one night in Gangtok first. Eat a light breakfast, drink water through the day, and skip alcohol the night before. At Nathu La, walk slowly, avoid running up the steps for photos, and keep your time on top short.

Turn back and go down if anyone has a severe headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual sleepiness or difficulty breathing at rest. Going down is the cure. People with heart or lung disease, pregnant travellers and anyone with a recent illness should ask a doctor before going above 4,000 m. Operators usually will not take children under 5 to Nathu La, and very young children are better off at the lake only.

sections.heading: What to wear and what to hire
paras: It can be pleasant in Gangtok and below freezing at Nathu La on the same morning. Dress in layers you can add and remove in the car.

Roadside shops before the lake rent knee-length coats and gumboots. Hire boots only if there is snow or slush on the ground, usually from December to March. In April, May, October and November, warm clothes from home are usually enough; in July and August, a rain layer matters more than a heavy coat.
list: Thermal top, fleece or sweater, and a windproof or down jacket.
Warm cap, gloves and a scarf or buff; the wind at the pass is the coldest part.
Trousers you can move in, and thick socks.
Closed shoes with good grip; boots with snow on the ground.
Sunglasses and sunscreen; the sun at 4,000 m burns quickly, especially on snow.
Water, a few snacks, lip balm and any medicines you use.

sections.heading: Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La
paras: Tsomgo Lake, also called Changu, lies at 3,753 m, about 40 km from Gangtok, in a bowl of steep slopes inside the Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary, an area of about 31 km² known for rhododendrons, junipers and silver fir. The lake usually freezes in mid-winter and is ringed with flowering rhododendrons in May. Mornings give the clearest water and sky; by midday cloud often rolls in. Yaks wait by the shore for rides and photos.

Baba Harbhajan Singh Mandir honours a soldier of the Punjab Regiment who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968; the army's account says he fell into a stream while escorting a mule column. Soldiers' legend holds that his spirit still guards the border and warns troops in dreams, and that his belongings were sent home by train each year. Tell this as the legend it is; the shrine is cared for by the army, and visitors leave water bottles to be blessed.

Nathu La, at 4,310 m, is a pass on the border with Tibet, and Indian and Chinese posts stand very close together here. It has a long history: surveyed by J. W. Edgar in 1873, used by the Younghusband expedition of 1903–04, sealed after the 1962 war, and scene of deadly clashes in 1967 that are remembered at the Sherathang memorial below. Border trade reopened through Nathu La in 2006. Follow army instructions on where you may walk and photograph; rules are strict and change without notice.

sections.heading: Best time of year for this trip
paras: April, May, October and November give the best mix of open roads, clear mornings and manageable cold. May adds rhododendrons; October and November usually bring the clearest skies. From December to March you may see the lake frozen and snow on the road, but Nathu La closes more often and some days the road is shut beyond the lake. In monsoon, from June to September, the road is usually open to Tsomgo but slides and cloud are common, and Nathu La is less reliable.

Whatever the month, leave early. Clear views come before 10 am, permit queues are shorter, and you will be back in Gangtok before the afternoon cloud and traffic. Check current status before you travel, as road and pass openings change daily.

faqs.q: How long is the Tsomgo and Nathu La trip from Gangtok
faqs.a: A full day of about 8–9 hours. Most cars leave Gangtok between 6:30 and 7:30 am and return between 3 and 4 pm. Tsomgo Lake is about 40 km from Gangtok and Nathu La about 55 km by road, but the climb is steep and slow, with permit checks and stops. Tsomgo and Baba Mandir alone take about 6–7 hours.

faqs.q: How much does a Nathu La car cost from Gangtok
faqs.a: About ₹6,500–9,000 per vehicle for Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La, indicative 2026, for a Gangtok-registered car carrying up to about five people. Tsomgo and Baba Mandir alone cost about ₹4,500–6,500. The Sikkim government has published fixed and maximum fares for these packages, so ask your agent for the current chart and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which days is Nathu La open for tourists
faqs.a: As we understand the rule, Nathu La is open to Indian tourists Wednesday to Sunday and closed on Monday and Tuesday. The army can close it on any day for snow, landslides or security reasons. Your agent needs your documents a day ahead to file the permit. Check current status before you travel, especially between December and March.

faqs.q: Can foreigners go to Tsomgo Lake
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals with a valid Sikkim Restricted Area Permit can visit Tsomgo Lake on a day permit arranged by a registered Gangtok agent, usually in a group of at least two. They cannot continue to Nathu La or, usually, beyond the lake. Ask the agent to confirm the stops in advance. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Nathu La safe for children and seniors
faqs.a: For healthy older children and fit seniors, usually yes, with care. Nathu La is 4,310 m high and reached in about three hours, so altitude sickness is possible. Operators usually will not take children under 5. Anyone with heart or lung disease should ask a doctor first. Walk slowly, keep the visit short and go down if anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: Do I need to hire boots and coats for Tsomgo
faqs.a: Only if there is snow or slush, usually December to March, or if you have not packed warm clothes. Coats and boots cost ₹100–300 per item to hire, indicative 2026, at roadside shops before the lake. In April, May, October and November, a warm jacket, cap, gloves and good shoes from home are usually enough.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Tsomgo Lake
faqs.a: For clear views and open roads, April, May, October and November. May brings flowering rhododendrons around the lake, and October and November the clearest skies. For a frozen lake and snow, go from January to March, accepting that Nathu La may be closed. Whatever the month, aim to reach the lake before 10 am, before cloud builds.

faqs.q: What is the story of Baba Harbhajan Singh
faqs.a: Harbhajan Singh was a soldier of the Punjab Regiment who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968; the army's account says he fell into a stream while escorting a mule column. Soldiers' legend holds that his spirit still guards the border and warns troops in dreams. The army maintains a shrine to him on the Tsomgo–Nathu La road.

faqs.q: Can I see China from Nathu La
faqs.a: Yes. Nathu La is a pass on the border between Sikkim and Tibet, and Indian and Chinese posts stand very close together. On a clear day you can see the fence line, the buildings on the far side and the mountains of Tibet's Chumbi Valley. Follow army instructions on where to stand and what you may photograph; rules are strict.
